planting.note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification into a permanently moist, humus-rich, shaded streambank or seep edge; the fleshy rootstock resents disturbance, so avoid division where possible.

directions: A tall, airy California and Cascade native for consistently moist, shaded sites such as streambanks, seeps, and forest floor, this species fills a niche few shade perennials occupy, with showy pink-purple racemes in late spring over ferny foliage. It will not tolerate summer drought even briefly, so give it a permanently moist site and heavy mulch to keep roots cool. Pair with ferns and sedges that can tolerate the same wet shade so the planting looks intentional once the corydalis dies back for the season.

planting.note: Sow in winter or early fall to catch a cold spell for stratification; plant in humus-rich but well-drained soil in part shade, since good drainage matters more for this species than for most Corydalis.

directions: A large, vigorous, salt-tolerant corydalis from East Asian coastal habitats, this species carries a strong ferny clump and a long late-winter-to-spring display of golden-yellow racemes, distinct in scale from the smaller species already common in cultivation. Its salt tolerance makes it a rare shade-garden option for coastal or roadside-salt-exposed sites where few other corydalis would survive. Let it self-sow to maintain a planting, since individual plants are short-lived, and expect foliage to emerge in fall and persist through winter in mild climates.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers 2-3 inches deep in fall under deciduous shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid summer irrigation over the dormant tubers.

directions: An exceptionally cold-hardy spring-ephemeral bulb from the Siberian Altai, in cultivation since the early 1800s, this species carries large, showy cream-to-bright-primrose-yellow flowers distinct from the pink, purple, and white forms already common in cultivation. Its Siberian origin makes it notably more cold-tolerant but correspondingly less heat-tolerant than most garden corydalis, so it suits northern gardens better than the warmer end of the typical range. Where grown near other spring-ephemeral corydalis, it can hybridize spontaneously, producing prized creamy, lilac-brushed seedlings.

planting.note: Direct-sow outdoors in fall for natural cold stratification into a rock garden, alpine trough, or shaded, consistently wet, cool bed with sharp winter drainage.

directions: A diminutive, true-blue-to-violet-flowered circumboreal species adapted to cold, wet, shaded tundra and boreal-forest conditions rather than woodland or steppe, this is a genuine novelty for rock garden and alpine-trough enthusiasts. Mimic its native wet-meadow or snowbank habitat with reliable moisture and dappled shade, giving sharp winter drainage despite the summer wetness it wants. Plant in a tight grouping rather than singly so the small blue-violet flowers register as a feature, offering true blue color in part shade for northern-climate and high-elevation gardens.
